label: Bonus Class 4
title: Tricky Words and Sentence Rules
bigIdea: Most English words can be sounded out, but some very common words keep old spellings and must be learned by heart. A sentence also has rules: a capital letter at the start, spaces between words and a full stop or question mark at the end.
bigIdeaAr: معظم كلمات الإنجليزية يمكن قراءتها بالأصوات، لكن بعض الكلمات الشائعة جداً احتفظت بتهجئة قديمة ويجب حفظها عن ظهر قلب. وللجملة أيضاً قواعد: حرف كبير في البداية، ومسافات بين الكلمات، ونقطة أو علامة استفهام في النهاية.
builtOn: Lessons 13-16: Today is... (days of the week), I can... / Can you...?, Where is it? (in, on, under), I have... (pets)
Phonics groups 7-8 (Lessons 13 and 15): first sight words (I, the, a, to, go) and review
Bonus Classes 1-3: vowel friends, sound twins (f/v, s/z buzz), blending and sound boxes

objectives.en: I can explain why some words are tricky: English spelling is very old.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أشرح لماذا بعض الكلمات خادعة: لأن تهجئة الإنجليزية قديمة جداً.

objectives.en: I can find the tricky part of a word and read and write the, to, was, said, you, he, my and have.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أجد الجزء الخادع في الكلمة، وأن أقرأ وأكتب the و to و was و said و you و he و my و have.

objectives.en: I can start a sentence with a capital letter, always write I as a capital, and leave spaces between words.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أبدأ الجملة بحرف كبير، وأن أكتب I كبيراً دائماً، وأن أترك مسافات بين الكلمات.

objectives.en: I can end a sentence with a full stop or a question mark facing the English way (?).
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أنهي الجملة بنقطة أو بعلامة استفهام باتجاهها الإنجليزي (?).

keyTerms.meaning: A common word with a part you cannot sound out, so you learn that part by heart: said, was.
The big form of a letter: A, B, T. Used at the start of a sentence, for I and for names and days.
The dot at the end of a telling sentence: I have a cat.
The mark at the end of a question: Can you swim?
The gap between two words, about one finger wide.

linguisticsCorner.title: English spelling is an old photo

facts.en: English spelling is like an old photo of the language. Long ago people said every letter. Then the way people spoke changed, but many spellings stayed the same.
facts.ar: تهجئة الإنجليزية مثل صورة قديمة للغة. قديماً كان الناس ينطقون كل حرف، ثم تغيّرت طريقة الكلام لكن كثيراً من الكلمات بقيت تُكتب كما كانت.

facts.en: Look at knife (Lesson 10). More than 1,000 years ago people really said the k: 'k-nee-f'. The sound disappeared, but the letter stayed.
facts.ar: انظر إلى كلمة knife (الدرس 10). قبل أكثر من 1000 سنة كان الناس ينطقون حرف k فعلاً. اختفى الصوت لكن الحرف بقي.

facts.en: When printing came to England (William Caxton, 1476), spellings slowly became fixed in books, while the vowel sounds of English kept changing for about 200 years. That is why many vowels look one way and sound another.
facts.ar: عندما وصلت الطباعة إلى إنجلترا (ويليام كاكستون عام 1476) بدأت التهجئة تثبت في الكتب شيئاً فشيئاً، بينما استمرّت أصوات الحركات في التغيّر نحو 200 سنة. لهذا تبدو حركات كثيرة بشكل وتُنطق بشكل آخر.

facts.en: The word 'the' was once written with an old letter called thorn (þ). Printers later used y in its place, so 'Ye Olde Shop' on old signs really means 'The Old Shop'.
facts.ar: كانت كلمة the تُكتب قديماً بحرف قديم اسمه «ثورن» (þ). ثم استعمل الطابعون حرف y مكانه، لذلك عبارة Ye Olde Shop على اللافتات القديمة تعني في الحقيقة The Old Shop.

facts.en: About 100 words make up roughly half of everything we read in English, and many of them are tricky (the, was, said, you). Learn them by heart and you can read a lot!
facts.ar: نحو 100 كلمة تشكّل تقريباً نصف كل ما نقرؤه بالإنجليزية، وكثير منها خادع (the و was و said و you). احفظها وستستطيع أن تقرأ الكثير!

arabicBridge.point: Arabic has tricky words too: هذا and لكن hide a long a that is not written, the ل in الشمس is written but not said, and عمرو has a silent و.
arabicBridge.pointAr: في العربية كلمات خادعة أيضاً: في هذا ولكن ألف تُنطق ولا تُكتب، واللام في الشمس تُكتب ولا تُنطق، وفي عمرو واو لا تُنطق.

arabicBridge.point: The th in the, this, that is the same sound as ذ (tongue between the teeth, with a buzz). It is not z or d.
arabicBridge.pointAr: صوت th في the و this و that هو صوت الذال نفسه (اللسان بين الأسنان مع طنين)، وليس زاياً ولا دالاً.

arabicBridge.arabic: لا توجد حروف كبيرة في العربية
arabicBridge.point: Arabic has no capital letters; its letters change shape by their place in the word instead. English letters do not change shape by place, but a sentence, the word I, names and days start with a capital.
arabicBridge.pointAr: لا توجد حروف كبيرة في العربية، بل تتغيّر أشكال الحروف بحسب مكانها في الكلمة. أما الحروف الإنجليزية فلا يتغيّر شكلها بحسب المكان، لكن الجملة وكلمة I والأسماء والأيام تبدأ بحرف كبير.

arabicBridge.point: Arabic is written right to left, so its question mark and comma face the other way. In English write ? and , the English way round.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تُكتب من اليمين إلى اليسار، لذلك علامة الاستفهام والفاصلة فيها مقلوبتان. في الإنجليزية نكتب ? و , باتجاههما الإنجليزي.

arabicBridge.english: Full stop (.) and spaces between words
arabicBridge.point: Same in both languages: a dot ends a sentence and a space comes between words. In English print the letters inside a word do not join, so the finger space between words must be clear.
arabicBridge.pointAr: متشابهتان في اللغتين: النقطة تنهي الجملة والمسافة تفصل الكلمات. لكن الحروف الإنجليزية المطبوعة لا تتّصل داخل الكلمة، لذلك يجب أن تكون مسافة الإصبع بين الكلمات واضحة.

commonErrors.why: Spelling tricky words by sound. Their tricky part must be learned by heart.

commonErrors.wrong: reading said as 'sa-id' and was as 'wass' (Lazy A)
commonErrors.why: Sounding out a word that does not follow the rules. Spot the heart part and remember it.
Arabic has no capitals, and English only uses them in a few places, so they are easy to forget. I is always a capital.
No capital at the start, no capital for the day and no full stop. Days and names always start with a capital in English.
Using the Arabic question mark, which faces the other way.
Saying ذ as z or d, as in some spoken dialects. Tongue between the teeth: ذ.
Forgetting spaces between words. Use a finger space.

teacher: Heart word cards (with the tricky part in red and a heart above it): the, to, I, was, said, you, he, she, we, my, have, go
Punctuation action cards: capital letter, finger space, full stop, question mark
student: Paper and a pencil, plus a red pencil or crayon if possible
Eight small paper cards for tricky words (made in class)
A full stop card (.) and a question mark card (?)

stages.name: Warm-up: Blend It or Not?
stages.method: Retrieval of blending + discovery hook (a word that breaks the rules)
stages.purpose: Warm up blending from Bonus Class 3, then discover that some words do not work with blending.
teacherSays: Blending Builders, welcome back! Arm out. Let's blend: h-o-t, hot! c-a-t, cat! r-u-n, run!
Now this one: s-a-i-d. Blend it: s-a-i-d... 'sa-id'? Hmm. Is that a word?
No! This word is said. It is a tricky word. It breaks the rules! Today we find out why, and how to beat tricky words.
And then we will learn the rules of a sentence, like a real writer.
teacherSaysAr: لنَدمج: hot و cat و run. والآن s-a-i-d... هل هذه كلمة؟
هذه كلمة said، وهي كلمة خادعة لا تتبع القواعد! اليوم نعرف السبب.
studentsDo: Arm-tap and blend 4 decodable words.
Try to blend said and notice that it doesn't work.
Guess which other words might be tricky.
tips: Make the failed blend funny ('sa-id? Who is Sa-id?'), so children feel curious, not stuck.

stages.name: Linguistics Corner: Why Are Some Words Tricky?
stages.nameAr: ركن اللغويات: لماذا بعض الكلمات خادعة؟
stages.method: Storytelling with real language history + sorting (decodable vs tricky)
stages.purpose: Understand that tricky spellings are fossils of old English, and tell decodable words from tricky ones.
teacherSays: Long, long ago, English people said every letter. Look at knife from Lesson 10. They said 'k-nee-f'! The k sound went away, but the letter stayed.
English spelling is like an old photo. Grandpa's photo shows him young, but today he looks different. The spelling shows how words sounded long ago!
When books were printed, spellings got stuck. But people's mouths kept changing.
Old signs say 'Ye Olde Shop'. Ye? That is really the! The old letter þ was printed like y.
Now be detectives: can we blend it, or is it tricky?
teacherSaysAr: قديماً كان الناس ينطقون كل حرف. في كلمة knife كانوا ينطقون k! اختفى الصوت وبقي الحرف.
التهجئة مثل صورة قديمة لجدّك: تُظهر كيف كانت الكلمات تُنطق قديماً.
studentsDo: Say knife the old way and the new way.
Sort words on the slide: Blend it (green) or Tricky (red).
Show a thumbs-up (blend it) or a heart shape with hands (tricky).

exercise.instructions: Can you blend it? Thumbs-up for blend it, a hand heart for tricky.
exercise.instructionsAr: هل تستطيع دمج أصواتها؟ ارفع إبهامك إذا استطعت، واصنع قلباً بيديك إذا كانت خادعة.

tips: Keep the history to a story; the dates are for the teacher (Caxton 1476; the big vowel change from about 1400 to 1700).
Stress the good news: most English words can be blended. Only some are tricky, and they are tricky only in one small part.

stages.name: Heart Words: Find the Tricky Part
stages.nameAr: كلمات القلب: اعثر على الجزء الخادع
stages.method: Heart Word method (mark regular parts, put a heart on the irregular part) + sound links to earlier Bonus Classes
stages.purpose: Learn the tricky words by seeing that most letters are regular and only one part must be learned by heart.
teacherSays: Tricky words are not all tricky! Look at said. s: normal. d: normal. Only ai is tricky: it says Quick E! s-e-d. We put a heart over ai, because we learn it by heart.
was: w is normal. a is tricky: it says Round O, not Lazy A. And s says z, with a buzz! woz.
the: th is the sound ذ. Tongue between your teeth and buzz. e is short and lazy: 'thuh'.
to: t is normal. o says oo. he, she, we, me: e says its name, ee! go and no: o says its name.
my: y says 'eye'. I: always a capital, says its name. have: h-a-v normal, the e is silent. Fun fact: English words almost never end in v, so we add an e!
you: the whole word is tricky. Learn it like a picture: y-o-u.
teacherSaysAr: الكلمة الخادعة ليست كلها خادعة! في said: الحرفان s و d عاديان، والجزء الخادع فقط ai الذي يُنطق مثل E السريعة. نضع قلباً فوقه لأننا نحفظه بالقلب.
th في the هي صوت الذال: اللسان بين الأسنان مع طنين.
studentsDo: Write each heart word on a card and draw a heart over the tricky part (in red if possible).
Read each word three times: point, say, write it in the air (sky-writing).
Say the with the tongue between the teeth in the mirror (ذ, not z or d).

exercise.instructions: Which part is tricky? Draw a heart over it and say how it sounds.
exercise.instructionsAr: أيّ جزء خادع؟ ارسم قلباً فوقه وقل كيف يُنطق.

items.answer: a (says o) and s (says z): woz

tips: 'was' sounds like 'woz' in British English and like 'wuz' (Grumpy U) in American English. Accept both; just not Lazy A.
Link to earlier Bonus Classes: s in was buzzes like z (Bonus 2 twins), ai in said is Quick E (Bonus 1).
Children who say 'ze' or 'de' for the: Gulf children usually say ذ naturally in Arabic; Egyptian children know it from Quran recitation and fusha. Point to that sound.

stages.name: Tricky Word Games: Flash, Snap and Look-Say-Cover-Write
stages.nameAr: ألعاب الكلمات الخادعة: الوميض والمطابقة وانظر-قل-غطِّ-اكتب
stages.purpose: Make tricky words automatic for reading and spelling through fast, repeated retrieval.
teacherSays: Flash game! A word flashes on the screen for one second. Shout it out!
Now Look, Say, Cover, Write, Check. Look at said. Say it. Cover it with your hand. Write it. Check: did you get the heart part?
Fill the gap! Read the sentence and choose the tricky word.
teacherSaysAr: لعبة الوميض: تظهر الكلمة ثانية واحدة، قلها بسرعة!
انظر، قل، غطِّ، اكتب، ثم تحقّق: هل كتبت الجزء الخادع صحيحاً؟
studentsDo: Read flashed words as fast as possible.
Do Look-Say-Cover-Write-Check for said, was, the and you.
Complete gap sentences on the slide in the chat or on paper.

exercise.instructions: Choose from the word bank and write the missing tricky word: the, was, said, you, to, he, my, have.
exercise.instructionsAr: اكتب الكلمة الخادعة المفقودة: the أو was أو said أو you أو to أو he أو my أو have.

items.prompt: Yesterday the cat ___ in the box.
___ dog is big. (it is my dog)
Sam is my friend. ___ can run.

tips: Note that two answers start a sentence (My, He): a perfect bridge to the capital-letter rule in the next stages.
Keep flash speed high but repeat the hardest words (said, was, you) more often.

stages.name: Arabic Bridge: Capitals, ? and ؟
stages.nameAr: جسر العربية: الحروف الكبيرة و? و؟
stages.method: Contrastive analysis of writing systems (Arabic vs English text side by side)
stages.purpose: Show what English sentences need that Arabic does not (capitals) and what faces the other way (? and ,).
teacherSays: Look at this Arabic sentence and this English sentence. What is the same? Both have spaces between words. Both have a dot at the end!
What is different? English has big letters and small letters. Arabic has no capital letters at all. Instead, Arabic letters change shape: ب ـبـ ـب.
Look at the question marks: ؟ and ?. They are mirror twins! Arabic goes right to left, so its question mark faces left. English goes left to right, so ? faces the other way.
Arabic has tricky words too! هذا: we say haadhaa, but the first long a is not written. الشمس: we write ل but we don't say it!
teacherSaysAr: ما المتشابه؟ المسافات بين الكلمات والنقطة في النهاية. ما المختلف؟ لا توجد حروف كبيرة في العربية.
علامتا الاستفهام ؟ و? توأمان في المرآة! وفي العربية أيضاً كلمات خادعة: هذا والشمس.
studentsDo: Find what is the same and what is different in the two sentences.
Draw ؟ and ? side by side on paper and show the camera.
Find the Arabic tricky part in هذا and الشمس.
tips: Many children write ؟ in English because their hand is used to it; the mirror-twins picture helps them remember.
Celebrate the shared rules (spaces, full stop): the child already knows half the sentence rules from Arabic.

stages.name: Sentence Doctor: Capital, Space, Stop!
stages.nameAr: طبيب الجمل: حرف كبير، مسافة، توقّف!
stages.method: Kinesthetic punctuation (actions for each rule) + error correction (Sentence Doctor)
stages.purpose: Learn the four sentence rules with actions, then find and fix mistakes in sentences.
teacherSays: Every sentence has rules. Let's do them with our bodies!
Capital letter: stand tall, arms up! Finger space: two fingers up between words. Full stop: stamp your foot or punch the air: stop! Question mark: shrug your shoulders and draw a hook in the air.
Let's read with actions: (stand tall) I have a cat (stamp)!
Now you are Sentence Doctors. These sentences are sick! Find what is wrong and make them better.
Remember: I is always a capital, even in the middle. Days and names start with a capital too: Monday, Sam.
teacherSaysAr: حرف كبير: قف طويلاً وارفع ذراعيك! مسافة: إصبعان بين الكلمات. نقطة: اضرب الأرض بقدمك. علامة استفهام: هزّ كتفيك وارسم خطافاً في الهواء.
أنتم أطباء الجمل: هذه الجمل مريضة، اعثروا على الخطأ وأصلحوه!
studentsDo: Do the four punctuation actions while the teacher reads sentences.
Find the mistake in each sick sentence and say what the cure is.
Write the corrected sentence and hold it up to the camera.

exercise.instructions: This sentence is sick. Find the mistake and write it correctly.
exercise.instructionsAr: هذه الجملة مريضة. اعثر على الخطأ واكتبها صحيحة.

items.answer: My dog is in the box.

tips: Ask 'What is the cure?' so children name the rule (capital, space, full stop, question mark), not just copy the right answer.
Questions in Level 1 start with Can, Where, What, How: if the sentence starts with one of these, it needs a question mark.

stages.name: Writer's Challenge: My Three Sentences
stages.method: Guided writing (production) + peer checking with a rules checklist
stages.purpose: Write real sentences using tricky words and all four sentence rules, then check a friend's work.
teacherSays: Now you are writers! Write three sentences about you.
Sentence 1 is about a pet: I have a... Sentence 2 is about the day: Today is... Sentence 3 is a question for a friend: Can you...?
Use the checklist: capital? spaces? full stop or question mark? tricky words spelled right?
Read your sentences to the group. Your friends give you a star for each rule you got right!
teacherSaysAr: أنتم الآن كتّاب! اكتبوا ثلاث جمل عن أنفسكم.
استعملوا قائمة التحقّق: حرف كبير؟ مسافات؟ نقطة أو علامة استفهام؟ الكلمات الخادعة صحيحة؟
studentsDo: Write three sentences using the frames.
Tick the checklist for each sentence.
Read the sentences aloud; friends answer the question and give stars.

exercise.instructions: Finish each sentence with your own idea. Check the four rules.
exercise.instructionsAr: أكمل كل جملة بفكرتك الخاصة، وتحقّق من القواعد الأربع.

items.answer: e.g. I have a cat. (capital I, full stop)
e.g. Today is Monday. (capital for the day, full stop)
e.g. My dog is big. (capital M, full stop)
e.g. Where is the ball? (question mark)
e.g. He said, 'I can run.' (tricky words he, said)

tips: Three sentences are enough for most children; items 4-6 are for fast finishers.
Peer stars should name the rule ('a star for your question mark'), so feedback teaches.

stages.name: Exit Ticket, Did You Know? and Goodbye
stages.purpose: Check tricky-word spelling and the sentence rules alone, and finish with a fact to share at home.
teacherSays: Exit ticket! Write the words and the sentence I say.
Did you know? Old signs in England say 'Ye Olde Shop', but ye is really the! The old letter thorn (þ) looked a bit like y, so printers used y. English spelling is full of secrets from the past.
Your mission at home: be a Sentence Doctor. Find a sentence in a book and show your family the capital letter and the full stop.
teacherSaysAr: هل تعلم؟ اللافتات القديمة في إنجلترا تقول Ye Olde Shop، لكن ye تعني the! الحرف القديم þ كان يشبه y قليلاً.
مهمتك في البيت: كن طبيب جمل! ابحث عن جملة في كتاب وأرِ عائلتك الحرف الكبير والنقطة.
studentsDo: Write 3 tricky words and 2 sentences.
Say goodbye with the actions: stand tall, 'Bye!', stamp.
tips: Note who misses capitals or uses ؟; remind them in Lessons 17-19 writing tasks with the action gestures.

exitTicket.instructions: Items 1-3: listen and write the tricky word. Items 4-5: listen and write the sentence with a capital letter and the right end mark.
exitTicket.instructionsAr: 1-3: استمع واكتب الكلمة الخادعة. 4-5: استمع واكتب الجملة بحرف كبير وعلامة النهاية الصحيحة.

homework.en: Heart Word Hunt and Sentence Doctor: find the, was, said and you in a book or on a box at home and count how many times you see them. Then write three sentences about your family, with capitals, spaces and full stops.
homework.ar: صيد كلمات القلب وطبيب الجمل: ابحث عن the و was و said و you في كتاب أو على علبة في البيت، وعُدّ كم مرة تراها. ثم اكتب ثلاث جمل عن عائلتك بحروف كبيرة ومسافات ونقاط.
tasks: Make heart word cards for the, was, said, you, to, he, my, have and read them every day.
Do Look-Say-Cover-Write-Check for said and was.
Write three sentences about your family (one must be a question).

support: Learn four heart words only (the, to, I, you) and add the rest in later warm-ups.
Give sentence frames with the capital letter and end mark already printed; the child fills the gap.
In Sentence Doctor, tell the child which rule is broken and ask them to fix it.
challenge: Find the tricky part in more words: of (f says v!), are, do, come.
Write a sentence with a name, a day and the word I: 'On Monday, Sam and I can swim.'
Find a silent letter in a word from the lessons (knife: k) and explain why it is there.

successCriteria: Sorts at least 6 of 8 words correctly as blend it or tricky.
Marks the tricky part in at least 6 of 9 heart words.
Spells said, was and you correctly in the exit ticket.
Writes three sentences with capital letters, finger spaces and the correct end mark, and I always as a capital.
watchFor: tricky words spelled by sound (sed, woz, yu)
tricky words sounded out when reading (sa-id)
the said as ze or de

teacherNotes: This class closes the Sound Lab strand: Bonus Classes 1-3 showed how regular English is; this one shows where it is not regular and why.
Use the heart word idea for every new tricky word in Lessons 17-20: mark the regular parts, put a heart on the tricky part.

History facts are simplified for children but accurate: knife had a pronounced k in Old English (cnif); printing arrived in England with William Caxton in 1476; þ (thorn) was replaced by y in early printing, giving 'Ye Olde'.
Keep the Arabic comparison respectful and balanced: Arabic has fewer tricky spellings than English, but it does have some (هذا، لكن، الشمس، عمرو).
Level 2 (Spelling Detectives) continues with digraphs such as sh, ch and th, including the two sounds of th (ث and ذ).
